explanation: Chaplin first played the Tramp in 1914. In Modern Times (1936), the Tramp's last film, audiences finally heard Chaplin's voice, singing a song in made-up gibberish.

claims.text: Charlie Chaplin created and played the Little Tramp.
Buster Keaton, Harold Lloyd and Stan Laurel did not create or play the Little Tramp.
Chaplin first played the Tramp on screen in 1914.
Modern Times (1936) was the Tramp's last film.
In Modern Times, audiences heard Chaplin's voice on screen for the first time, singing a song in nonsense words.

writerNotes: Self-check 9.3. Lint: clean. Claims: every claim listed, risk at or above the C26 floor; the schema's riskReason list has no only or counterintuitive, so such claims carry the nearest listed reason. Datasets: no pinned dataset covers film or TV facts, so every high-risk claim here needs checker evidence from the web. Rival test: Stan Laurel was Chaplin's understudy in Fred Karno's troupe, and Keaton and Lloyd were the other great silent clowns, but none of them played the Tramp. Nothing argues against Chaplin. Volatility: evergreen; no time words; nothing depends on events after mid-2026. Regional: the work is known worldwide and the options need no single country's local knowledge. Style: Oxford spelling, straight single quotes, plain hyphens, explanation of 26 words. Myths: claims screened against myths.json, no match. Mystery and encore: not applicable to a practice item. Doubts: the Tramp's debut film is given as Kid Auto Races at Venice or Mabel's Strange Predicament, both from 1914, so the claim names only the year.

evidence.restatement: Chaplin devised the Tramp (the Little Tramp) and played him across his comedies.
The Tramp was Chaplin's own character; Keaton, Lloyd and Laurel had their own screen personas and never played him.
The Tramp's first screen appearances came in Keystone shorts released in February 1914, such as Kid Auto Races at Venice.
